analysis.one_liner: Caps all consumer credit rates and fees at 36% a year, covering payday, title, and overdraft charges.
analysis.headline: The 36% rate cap never got a hearing, markup, or vote; it expired when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal lending law to bar any consumer loan or credit line with combined interest and fees above 36% a year. The cap counts every charge — payday fees, car title loan charges, overdraft fees, late fees, and credit insurance — so lenders could not repackage the cost into add-on fees. Loans made above the cap would be unenforceable, lenders would have to return everything they collected, and violators would face criminal penalties. State attorneys general could enforce it. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never taken up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income borrowers who use small-dollar credit: payday borrowers paying around 400% annual rates, car title borrowers around 300%, and bank customers paying overdraft fees that annualize into the hundreds or thousands of percent. Millions of other consumers pay overdraft fees, and the bill's findings put annual spending on high-cost overdraft loans at roughly $17 billion and payday loans at up to $7 billion.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any consumer credit — including open-end credit plans — with a combined interest and fee rate above 36% per year, superseding other law.

Counts every charge toward the cap, including late fees, overdraft fees, over-limit fees, cash advance fees, and credit insurance premiums, so lenders cannot hide the true rate in add-on fees; the CFPB may adjust calculation rules but may not exempt lenders from the cap.

Cites findings that consumers pay about $17 billion a year in high-cost overdraft loans and up to $7 billion in storefront and online payday loans, with average rates around 400% for payday and up to 3,500% annualized for bank overdraft loans.

Makes loans above the cap void and unenforceable: creditors and debt collectors must return all principal, interest, and fees collected, and borrowers can raise the violation as a defense to collection at any time, with no deadline.

Adds enforcement teeth: up to 1 year in prison and a fine of the greater of triple the accrued debt or $50,000 per violation, plus the power for state attorneys general to sue in federal court within three years.
Leaves stronger state interest-rate protections in place rather than overriding them.

analysis.who_pays: Payday, car title, and high-cost online installment lenders, whose core products become illegal, and banks and credit card issuers that would lose overdraft, late, and high-fee revenue. The bill's honest trade-off is that some borrowers with poor credit might lose access to any formal small-dollar loan if lenders cannot price for the risk at 36%.

drawbacks.text: A hard 36% all-in cap can price high-risk borrowers out of legal credit entirely; lenders argue the cost of underwriting small, short-term loans exceeds what 36% of a small balance yields, so the people who relied on payday loans may be left with no option at all — the bill responds by encouraging low-fee, installment-style alternatives but does not create them.

Including overdraft and late fees in a 36% annualized cap is aggressive: banks earn a large share of consumer fee revenue from these charges, and a miscalculation could push ordinary credit card accounts or accounts with a single overdraft over the legal line.

The penalty structure is severe for a rate cap — up to a year in prison and fines of the greater of three times the accrued debt or $50,000 for each violation — and voiding loans means even a subsequent purchaser of the debt must return everything collected.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of consumers paying triple-digit or annualized rates in the hundreds of percent, the cap would be a large, direct saving, and the bill closes the loopholes that let high-cost lenders operate in all 50 states. The real cost is credit access for the riskiest borrowers, which the bill addresses with encouragement of alternatives but no replacement program. On balance the design is consumer-protective and unusually airtight (no exemptions, fee-inclusive, enforceable), with the main open question being what fills the gap for borrowers with no 36%-capable option.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on March 24, 2015, with 17 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services that same day; that referral was the only action of its entire two-year life.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded, and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, car title, and high-cost online lenders and the banks collecting overdraft and late fees kept a business that the bill's findings put in the tens of billions of dollars a year; borrowers kept paying the same rates. The outcome favored the financial firms, not because the bill lost a vote, but because the committee majority never allowed one.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did

sides.party_line_note: All 27 supporters — the sponsor and 26 cosponsors — were House Democrats, and the Republican majority that controlled the Financial Services Committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: The cap would outlaw loans averaging around 400% annual interest, a market the bill's findings put at up to $7 billion a year. Their business model depends on charging rates the bill would make criminal, so their interest runs directly against the borrowers the bill protects.
Loans averaging around 300% annual interest secured by vehicle titles would exceed the 36% cap and become void, with repossession rights unenforceable. They profit from borrowers' emergencies.

industries.industry: Banks and credit unions (overdraft and deposit-advance fees)
industries.note: Overdraft fees count toward the cap, and the bill's findings estimate consumers pay about $17 billion a year in high-cost overdraft loans, with annualized rates up to 3,500%. Banks would lose a large, recurring fee stream that falls hardest on low-balance customers.
Triple-digit-rate online installment loans, which the bill notes exploit rate-exportation loopholes across state lines, would be capped nationwide with no exemptions.

The cap covers open-end credit plans, but most standard credit card pricing sits below 36% all-in, so the effect on mainstream cards is small; subprime and fee-heavy cards would be constrained, and late and over-limit fees would count toward the cap.
